name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
title: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
answer: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology turn CT and MRI scans into physical, patient-specific replicas of organs, bones, and vascular structures. These models support surgical planning, implant sizing, medical education, and patient consent discussions. The practice sits at the boundary of diagnostic imaging, additive manufacturing, and clinical engineering. Radiologists and technologists work with surgeons and biomedical engineers to decide which cases benefit from a printed model. The field includes both hospital point-of-care printing and models produced by external service bureaus.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology turn CT and MRI scans into physical, patient-specific replicas of organs, bones, and vascular structures. These models support surgical planning, implant sizing, medical education, and patient consent discussions. The practice sits at the boundary of diagnostic imaging, additive manufacturing, and clinical engineering. Radiologists and technologists work with surgeons and biomedical engineers to decide which cases benefit from a printed model. The field includes both hospital point-of-care printing and models produced by external service bureaus.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The workflow begins with DICOM image data from CT, MRI, or sometimes ultrasound. Segmentation software runs on radiology workstations, often with GPU acceleration for AI-assisted tools. The resulting 3D mesh is exported as an STL or 3MF file and sent to a printer, commonly a material jetting, stereolithography, or fused deposition modeling machine. Print materials range from rigid resins for bone to flexible polymers for vessels and soft tissue. Post-processing equipment includes support removal baths, UV curing chambers, and sterilization systems for intraoperative use.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A radiologist or trained technologist first selects the appropriate imaging series and confirms slice thickness and contrast. Segmentation isolates the anatomy of interest, either manually, with thresholding and region growing, or with AI models that automatically label organs and vessels. The segmented volume is converted into a watertight mesh, smoothed, and hollowed or split for printing. The printed model is then checked against the source images for dimensional accuracy and anatomical fidelity. For surgical use, the model may be sterilized and brought into the operating room.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Patient imaging data used for printing is protected health information and requires the same consent and security controls as any radiology study. In the United States, point-of-care 3D printed anatomical models are generally treated as medical devices, and the FDA has issued guidance on software and manufacturing quality. Risks include geometric error from poor segmentation, material failure during surgery, and unclear liability when a model contributes to a wrong-site or wrong-size decision. Provenance should record the source DICOM study, segmentation software and version, AI model if used, and printer settings so that a model can be traced back to its origin.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: AI segmentation is reducing the time needed to create printable models from hours to minutes, which makes point-of-care printing practical for more emergency and trauma cases. Hospitals are moving toward centralized 3D printing labs with quality management systems and dedicated biomedical staff. Research is exploring multi-material prints that mimic tissue stiffness and even bioprinted constructs for implants. Digital twins, where the printed model is paired with a simulation of the same anatomy, are beginning to connect preoperative planning with intraoperative navigation. Regulatory frameworks are expected to become more specific as the volume of printed models grows.
